---
title: Search your app's data
description: Declare which fields of a collection are indexed, query them from a view, and know what it costs, what it guarantees and where it stops.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

**Task:** find records by the words in them — notes that mention "invoice",
titles that start with "roa" — without reading every record in the app.

Each node that holds a replica of the app keeps a full-text index
([tantivy](https://github.com/quickwit-oss/tantivy)) of the tables that declare
search fields, built from the state it holds. The index is derived data: it is
never replicated and never part of the app's state. A node on an encrypted data
disk (mero-tee's, whose key comes from mero-kms) keeps it on that disk, so it
survives a restart; any other node keeps it in memory. A query reads the page of
hits, never the table.

## Declare and query

Declare the fields to index on the table itself, and the host keeps the index
from the app's state:

```rust
#[derive(Record)]
#[table(key = "id", search = ["title", "body"])]
pub struct Note {
    pub id: String,
    pub title: String,
    pub body: String,
}

#[app::view]
pub fn find_notes(&self, text: String) -> app::Result<Vec<Note>> {
    let found = self.notes.search(&text, SearchOpts::default().limit(20))?;
    Ok(found.items.into_iter().map(|f| f.record).collect())
}
```

- The state ABI lists the fields (`state.search`: table to fields, camelCase).
  Text fields are indexed; a list of strings is joined; anything else is skipped.
- Every record of the table is one document. Each replica derives its index
  from the record keys the entries it applied touched, else from a scan of the
  table, before a view reads; nothing enters the log.
- `Table::search(text, SearchOpts)` queries through the WIT `search` interface
  (`SearchMode::{Words, Prefix, Substring, Fuzzy}`, a cursor and a limit of 1 to
  100) and reads each hit's record back; a hit whose record is gone is skipped.
  Only views search; any other run traps `HostDenied`. A call of a declared view
  runs as a strong view, so it may search too.
- A view's searches see exactly the state its reads see, the applied index the
  view runs at: no hit for a record written after it, and no record deleted
  after it missing. The node brings the index up to that state before the
  view's first search, on the view's own thread, and the view then searches a
  point-in-time copy of it, so a write applied while the view runs, and other
  views searching meanwhile, change nothing it sees. The index is never behind
  the state a view reads, so a view never waits for indexing to catch up; the
  first search of a view after writes pays for indexing what they touched.
- The test harness (`TestApp`) answers searches with the node's own index
  (`calimero-search`), built from the view's state: the same words, ranking,
  scores, snippets and pages a node gives for that state.

## Limits

- One index per table, over the fields its `#[table(search = [..])]` names.
- A query is at most 256 bytes and 4 KiB encoded; a page at most 100 hits; a
  cursor at most 10,000 deep.
- A view makes at most 32 searches (`MAX_SEARCHES_PER_RUN`); past it a search
  answers `"too many searches in one run"`. Each search costs the view fuel for
  the documents it matched and the hits it returns
  ([What host work costs](/protocol/limits/#what-host-work-costs)).
- Fuzzy matching is edit distance 1 on words: no stemming, no synonyms, no
  phonetics. Substring search needs 3 characters.
- Scores are per app (each index has its own term statistics).
- A stale view on a replica that is behind searches the state that replica
  has applied.
- A new release keeps the index of every table whose search fields it keeps;
  a new table, or one whose fields changed, is built from state on the first
  view after it, about 0.1 ms a document.
- The first view after a restart compares the index with the state and indexes
  again only the records that changed (on a node that keeps indexes on disk; a
  node that keeps them in memory builds them again). So does the first view
  after the app moves to a node, which has no index of it yet.

## Operating it

There is nothing to configure: search is on for every app that declares an
index, and its indexes live on the nodes that serve its views (on disk under
`<data dir>/search` when merod runs with `--kms-disk-evidence`, else in memory).
A node keeps the touched entities of the last 4096 entries per app
(`TOUCHED_RING`); a view after a longer gap compares each index with a scan of
the state and indexes only what differs.
